script.opening: (Frightened.) "Doctor, I woke up and half my face has gone — my eye won't close properly and my mouth's pulling to one side, tea's dribbling out. I'm 39 and I'm pregnant and I'm terrified I'm having a stroke. My nan had one and this is exactly how hers looked. Please — is this a stroke? What do I do?"

facts.text: Noticed on waking at 7am. Left side of the face is drooped. You cannot close the left eye fully; the left corner of your mouth droops and tea dribbles out.

facts.topic: Forehead — answer if asked to try in a mirror
facts.text: When you try to raise your eyebrows, the left eyebrow does not move and the left side of your forehead stays smooth; the right side wrinkles normally.

Arms and legs feel normal and strong; you can hold both arms out. Speech is clear (a bit slurred only because the lip will not move). No double vision or loss of vision, no numbness elsewhere, no dizziness, no headache, no trouble swallowing, walking normally.
Ache behind the left ear yesterday. Food tastes "odd" on the left of your tongue. Loud noises sound harsh in the left ear. No rash or blisters in or around the ear.

28 weeks, first baby, all well so far. Baby moving normally today. No headache, no visual disturbance, no swelling of face or hands, no tummy pain. Booking blood pressure was normal; you have not had it checked for three weeks.
No high blood pressure, diabetes or heart problems. Never smoked. Medicines: pregnancy vitamins only. No allergies.
39, works in HR. Husband Raj is at home with you and can drive.

You are frightened that something is wrong with the baby, or that any treatment will harm it. Also: "Will my face stay like this for the wedding photos in June?" Say these only if the doctor asks what worries you most, or mentions treatment.

Very frightened at first, talking fast. If the doctor asks you to try specific movements, do them and report back. If they explain why the forehead matters and that this looks much more like Bell's palsy than a stroke, you calm noticeably — but still want to know about the baby. If treatment is mentioned, ask: "Is it safe in pregnancy?"

ice.ideas: "I think I'm having a stroke, like my nan."
ice.concerns: Underneath (only if asked): whether the baby is okay, and whether your face will recover.
ice.expectations: To know whether it is a stroke and what to do right now. You expect to be seen.

cues: "My nan had a stroke and this is exactly how hers looked." — say in the opening.
"Is it safe for the baby?" — ask when any treatment is mentioned.

checkpoints.text: Applies the KEY discriminator: establishes whether the FOREHEAD is involved — forehead involvement (can’t raise eyebrow) with isolated facial weakness points to a lower-motor-neurone (Bell’s) palsy, whereas forehead SPARING + other deficits suggests an upper-motor-neurone (stroke) lesion — knowing the sign is not absolute (a brainstem lesion can involve the forehead), so any other deficit means the stroke pathway — and screens FAST/other neurology

Still arranges PROMPT same-day assessment to EXCLUDE stroke and examine fully (confirm forehead sign, no limb/speech/visual/sensory deficit), rather than diagnosing Bell’s purely over the phone — sudden facial weakness warrants urgent face-to-face evaluation

Recognises and treats BELL’S appropriately: early corticosteroids (ideally within 72 hours of onset) where indicated, and crucially EYE PROTECTION (lubricating drops/ointment, taping the eye at night) because incomplete eye closure risks exposure keratopathy — a commonly-missed essential

Considers the differential/special cases: Ramsay Hunt syndrome (vesicles in/around the ear, severe pain — needs antivirals + steroids), Lyme disease, parotid lesions, and bilateral/other-cranial-nerve involvement (which would change the picture); and accounts for PREGNANCY (Bell’s commoner; involve obstetric advice on steroids without delaying them; check blood pressure and urine protein at 28 weeks for pre-eclampsia — NICE NG133)

Gives an accurate PROGNOSIS: most people with Bell’s recover well, especially with early treatment — directly addressing the disfigurement fear — while being honest that recovery can take weeks to months
Responds to the stroke terror with the reassuring forehead-sign reasoning, and surfaces/addresses the unspoken pregnancy fear (the baby) — not just the facial diagnosis
Balances genuine reassurance (very likely Bell’s, good recovery) with the honesty that she still needs urgent assessment to be sure

Safety-nets and follows up: same-day assessment; red flags that would change urgency (limb weakness, speech change, vomiting, drowsiness, vesicles, eye pain/visual change → urgent/999); eye-care instructions; pregnancy-safe treatment plan with blood pressure and urine protein checked; review and recovery expectations

worked.lbl: Hear the fear, then the key question
worked.txt: "I can hear how frightening this is, and a drooping face naturally makes everyone think stroke — so let me ask the one question that helps most: can you raise your eyebrows and wrinkle your forehead on the drooped side? Try now. … You CAN’T move that forehead. Okay — that’s actually reassuring, and let me explain why."

"With a stroke, the forehead usually still works because it gets signals from both sides of the brain — so the forehead is spared. When the WHOLE side of the face including the forehead is affected, like yours, it points instead to a nerve problem in the face itself, called Bell’s palsy. That, plus no weakness in your arm or leg and normal speech, makes a stroke much less likely. The ache behind your ear and the recent cold fit Bell’s too."

"Now — I’m reassured, but I’m not going to diagnose this down the phone. Sudden facial weakness needs you examined properly today, to be completely sure it’s not a stroke and to start the right treatment. So I’m arranging that urgently. Reassured, but careful — both at once."

"One really important thing right now: if your eye won’t close fully, it can dry out and get damaged. So use lubricating eye drops often during the day, ointment and gently tape the eye shut at night, and wear sunglasses outside. Protecting that eye matters as much as anything else — it’s easy to overlook."

"I suspect part of you is also frightened for the baby — is that right? Let me reassure you: Bell’s is actually a bit more common in pregnancy and it does NOT harm the baby. There’s a steroid treatment that works best started early, and we’ll use it safely with advice from the pregnancy team. I’ll also check your blood pressure and a urine sample when you come in today, because this can occasionally go along with high blood pressure in pregnancy. Your baby is not in danger from this."

"And the outlook: most people with Bell’s recover well, especially treated early — it can take some weeks, occasionally a few months, but the great majority get their face back. If meanwhile you DO get arm or leg weakness, slurred speech, drowsiness, a blistery rash around the ear, or eye pain or vision changes — that’s 999/urgent. Otherwise, let’s get you seen today, protect that eye, and start treatment. You feared the worst; the likely answer is far kinder."

f.learning: Sudden one-sided facial droop forces the Bell’s-vs-stroke discrimination, and the KEY sign is the FOREHEAD: in a lower-motor-neurone (Bell’s) palsy the forehead is INVOLVED (can’t raise the eyebrow) because the upper face has bilateral cortical innervation, whereas an upper-motor-neurone (stroke) lesion SPARES the forehead — a strong clue but not absolute, since a brainstem stroke can involve the whole face. Forehead involvement with isolated facial weakness and no other neurology (normal limbs, speech, vision), plus supportive features (post-auricular ache, altered taste, recent virus), points to Bell’s — but sudden facial weakness still needs prompt same-day assessment to exclude stroke and examine fully. Treat Bell’s with early corticosteroids (ideally within 72 h) and — crucially and commonly missed — EYE PROTECTION (lubrication, night taping) to prevent exposure keratopathy; consider Ramsay Hunt (vesicles, severe pain → add antivirals), Lyme and other causes, and manage pregnancy with obstetric input (without delaying steroids), checking blood pressure and urine for pre-eclampsia. The examinable hidden agenda is twofold fear — a relative’s stroke and an unspoken fear for the baby; reassure with the forehead-sign reasoning, address the pregnancy fear, give the good prognosis (most recover well), and safety-net stroke/Ramsay-Hunt/eye red flags.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG127 (suspected neurological conditions) · NICE NG128 (stroke and TIA) · NICE NG133 (hypertension in pregnancy)
knowledge.summary: Whole-hemiface weakness including the forehead, with no other neurology, points to Bell’s palsy — but sudden facial weakness still needs same-day examination. Treat early with prednisolone, protect the eye, and in pregnancy check for pre-eclampsia.

points.t: The upper face has bilateral cortical supply, so a stroke usually spares the forehead, while a lower motor neurone palsy weakens the whole side. It is a clue, not a complete test: a brainstem lesion can produce a whole-face palsy, so any other neurological sign goes to the stroke pathway (NICE NG128) whatever the forehead shows.

Acute unilateral lower motor neurone facial weakness developing over hours, often with ache behind the ear, altered taste or hyperacusis, after a viral illness. It is a diagnosis of exclusion: a typical story and an examination that is normal apart from the face.

Start oral prednisolone as early as possible, ideally within 72 hours of onset; regimen per local formulary and BNF. In pregnancy, discuss with the obstetric team but do not let the discussion delay treatment. Antivirals are not routine and never used alone.

Incomplete eye closure risks exposure keratopathy. Lubricating drops by day, ointment at night, gentle taping or a moisture chamber, and sunglasses. A painful or red eye or change in vision needs same-day ophthalmology.

Bell’s palsy is more common in late pregnancy, and published case series link it with gestational hypertension and pre-eclampsia. Check blood pressure and urine for protein at the same-day review and manage per NICE NG133.

Ramsay Hunt syndrome (ear or palate vesicles, severe ear pain, hearing loss, vertigo) needs antiviral plus steroid and urgent ENT input. Also consider Lyme disease, parotid masses and bilateral palsy. Review if not improving by about 3 weeks and consider facial-palsy referral at about 3 months if recovery is incomplete (local pathway); NICE NG127: consider specialist assessment for synkinesis from about 5 months.

model.text: Hello, is that Priya Naidu? It’s Dr Evans from the surgery — I understand your face has changed this morning. Tell me what’s happened.
I woke up and half my face has gone. My eye won’t close properly and tea’s dribbling out. I’m pregnant and I’m terrified I’m having a stroke. My nan had one and this is exactly how she looked.
That sounds really frightening, especially after seeing what happened to your nan. I’m going to ask a few quick questions that will tell us a lot, and then I’ll explain what I think. Is that okay?
model.why: Acknowledges fear and sets a brief, purposeful structure

model.text: Yes. Please.
Can you lift both arms out in front of you and hold them there — does either drift down or feel weak? And any numbness, change in your vision, or trouble finding words?
model.why: Screens for FAST features and other focal neurology

model.text: My arms are fine. I can see fine, and I’m talking normally — it’s just my mouth feels odd.
Good. Now one really useful test: look up at the ceiling and try to raise your eyebrows and wrinkle your forehead. Does the left side of your forehead move?
model.why: Applies the forehead discriminator by remote instruction

model.text: No… the left side doesn’t move at all. The right side does.
Thank you. Any ache around your ear, change in taste, sounds seeming louder, or any blisters or rash in or around the ear? Any hearing loss or dizziness?
model.why: Looks for supportive Bell’s features and screens for Ramsay Hunt

model.text: An ache behind the ear yesterday, and tea tasted a bit strange this morning. No rash that I can feel. Hearing’s fine.
And any recent illness?
I’ve just had a cold.
You mentioned being pregnant. Alongside the stroke worry, is there anything on your mind about the baby?
That’s the thing I can’t stop thinking about. What if something’s wrong with the baby, or whatever you give me hurts it? And will my face stay like this?

Let me explain what I’m thinking. In a stroke the forehead usually keeps working, because it gets signals from both sides of the brain. When the whole side of the face is weak, including the forehead, and arms, speech and vision are normal, it points to a problem with the facial nerve itself — Bell’s palsy. The ear ache, taste change and your cold fit that too.
model.why: Explains the forehead reasoning in plain language

model.text: So it’s not a stroke?

It looks much more like Bell’s palsy, which is reassuring. But I won’t diagnose it over the phone. Sudden facial weakness needs examining properly today, so I’d like to see you at the surgery this morning. If at any point your arm or leg goes weak or your speech changes, that’s 999 straight away.
model.why: Balances reassurance with same-day face-to-face assessment to exclude stroke

model.text: Okay. And the baby?

Bell’s palsy is a bit more common in pregnancy, and it doesn’t harm the baby. When I see you I’ll also check your blood pressure and a urine sample, because in pregnancy it’s sensible to check for high blood pressure alongside this.
model.why: Answers the baby fear and screens for pre-eclampsia

model.text: If it is Bell’s, the treatment that helps most is a short course of steroid tablets started within three days. It’s used in pregnancy when the benefit is clear, and I’ll check the plan with the maternity team today so you’re not left wondering. How do you feel about that?
model.why: Shared decision on steroids with obstetric input, inviting her view

model.text: If it’s safe for the baby, I want it. I just want my face back.

Most people with Bell’s recover well, especially with early treatment. It can take weeks, sometimes a few months. The other really important thing is your eye: until it closes properly it can dry out and get damaged. Use lubricating drops through the day, ointment at night, gently tape it shut when you sleep, and wear sunglasses outside.
model.why: Gives prognosis and essential eye-protection advice

model.text: I wouldn’t have thought of the eye.

So: come in this morning, and I’ll examine you, check your blood pressure and urine, and start treatment if it’s Bell’s. Call 999 for weakness in an arm or leg, slurred speech or drowsiness. Contact us the same day for blisters around the ear, a painful or red eye, or change in vision, a severe headache, or feeling unwell with swelling or visual disturbance.
model.why: Specific stroke, Ramsay Hunt, eye and pre-eclampsia safety-net

model.text: Okay. I can get a lift in.
Just so I know I’ve explained it clearly — what’s the plan for this morning, and what would make you ring 999?
Come in now, protect my eye, and 999 if my arm or speech goes. And it’s probably not a stroke.
Exactly. You were right to ring. I’ll see you shortly.
model.why: Closes with a clear next step

social.t: Facial asymmetry, drooling and difficulty eating can be distressing and socially isolating. Acknowledge it and give a realistic recovery timeline.
A relative’s stroke shapes how she reads her own symptoms. Addressing that story directly reduces panic and improves engagement with the plan.

legal.t: If she cannot close the eye or protect it, or her vision is affected by drops or ointment, advise her not to drive until she can do so safely and meets the DVLA eyesight standard.
If she works and needs time off, a fit note can be issued; pregnancy-related protections at work continue alongside.

professional.t: Telephone triage can guide urgency but cannot replace examination for sudden neurological symptoms. Document the questions asked, the answers, and the plan for same-day review.
Weigh benefit and risk, check the BNF, involve the maternity team, and record the shared decision (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024).

community.t: Inform her midwife or maternity unit so blood pressure and fetal wellbeing are followed up at routine and additional antenatal visits.
Facial Palsy UK offers information on eye care, exercises and recovery, and support for people with persistent weakness.

redFlags: Limb weakness, speech or visual disturbance, ataxia or sensory loss — stroke pathway, 999
Vesicles in or around the ear or palate, severe ear pain, hearing loss or vertigo — Ramsay Hunt
Headache, visual disturbance, swelling or raised BP in pregnancy — possible pre-eclampsia
psychosocial: Pregnancy at 28 weeks and her fear for the baby
Her nan’s stroke and how it shapes her fear
Practical ability to attend today; eating, drinking and eye care at home
ice: Idea: “I’m having a stroke, like my nan”
Concern: harm to the baby from the illness or its treatment; permanent disfigurement
Expectation: to know whether it’s a stroke and what to do now

playbook.diagnosis: Probable Bell’s palsy: the whole left face including the forehead is weak, with no limb, speech or visual deficit — but it still needs same-day examination: “This looks much more like a facial-nerve problem than a stroke. I want to examine you today to be sure.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “The facial nerve is like a cable from the brain to the face. In Bell’s palsy the cable itself becomes swollen and stops carrying signals to that whole side of the face — forehead included. In a stroke, the forehead usually keeps working because it gets a back-up signal from the other side of the brain.”

management.reflectIce: “You were frightened this was a stroke like your nan’s, and worried for the baby. The signs point to Bell’s palsy, which doesn’t harm the baby — and we’ll check you properly today.”
management.psychosocial: Make same-day attendance easy, give practical eye-care steps she can do now, and link in the maternity team so she isn’t carrying the pregnancy worry alone.
sharedPlan: Same-day face-to-face examination; BP and urine protein
Prednisolone within 72 hours per formulary and BNF, agreed with the maternity team
Eye protection: drops, night ointment, taping, sunglasses
safetyNet: 999 for limb weakness, speech change or drowsiness
Same-day contact for ear vesicles, eye pain or visual change, severe headache; review if no improvement

pitfalls.intro: This telephone station is about safe triage under emotional pressure: recognise the likely Bell’s palsy, still get her examined today, and deal with two fears — stroke and the baby.

items.fail: Confirming Bell’s palsy on the phone and posting a prescription without examination.
items.why: Sudden facial weakness needs examination to exclude stroke and Ramsay Hunt. The forehead clue is not a complete test — brainstem lesions can mimic it.
items.fix: “It looks much more like Bell’s, but I want to examine you this morning.”

items.why: Exposure keratopathy is a preventable complication and a commonly missed checkpoint.
items.fix: Drops by day, ointment and taping at night, sunglasses — and same-day review for eye pain or visual change.

items.fail: Refusing or delaying steroids because she is pregnant.
items.why: Benefit is time-dependent. Pregnancy calls for obstetric input, not automatic refusal.
items.fix: Offer prednisolone within 72 hours and agree it with the maternity team the same day.

items.fail: Treating the face in isolation and not checking blood pressure.
items.why: Bell’s palsy in late pregnancy has been linked with pre-eclampsia; missing it is a safety failure.
items.fix: BP and urine protein at the same-day review, and pre-eclampsia symptoms in the safety-net.

items.fail: Answering only the stroke question and never asking about the baby.
items.why: “Does not explore the patient’s concerns.” The unspoken pregnancy fear drives her distress.
items.fix: “Is there anything on your mind about the baby?”

items.why: “Language not easily understood by the patient”, especially on the phone.
items.fix: “In a stroke the forehead usually keeps working because it gets signals from both sides of the brain.”

items.fail: Safety-net limited to “call back if worse”.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting is standard failing feedback when stroke is on the differential.
items.fix: Name 999 symptoms (limb, speech, drowsiness) and same-day symptoms (ear vesicles, eye pain, visual change, severe headache).

timeMap.d: Let her describe it. Name the fear of stroke and her nan’s history before starting questions.
Arms, speech, vision, sensation. Forehead test by instruction. Ear ache, taste, vesicles, hearing, vertigo, recent illness.
“Is there anything on your mind about the baby?” Also the fear of lasting disfigurement.
Forehead reasoning, same-day examination, BP and urine, prednisolone with obstetric input, eye protection, prognosis.
999 for limb or speech change. Same-day for vesicles, eye symptoms, pre-eclampsia symptoms. Teach-back.

wordPics.fail: Diagnoses stroke and sends to hospital without assessing, or diagnoses Bell’s by phone with no same-day examination; never checks the forehead; forgets the eye; ignores the pregnancy or refuses steroids outright; no safety-net.
wordPics.pass: Screens for stroke features and checks the forehead; arranges same-day examination; plans prednisolone within 72 hours and eye protection; reassures about the baby; gives 999 red flags.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: explains the forehead clue in plain words while acknowledging its limits; screens for Ramsay Hunt; checks BP and urine for pre-eclampsia; involves the maternity team without delaying treatment; addresses disfigurement with an honest prognosis; confirms the plan with teach-back.

avoid.dont: “It’s definitely not a stroke, it’s just Bell’s palsy.”
avoid.instead: “It looks much more like Bell’s palsy, which is reassuring — but I want to examine you today to be sure.”
avoid.why: Telephone certainty is unsafe; sudden facial weakness needs examination.

avoid.dont: “We can’t give steroids because you’re pregnant.”
avoid.instead: “Steroids are used in pregnancy when the benefit is clear — I’ll agree the plan with the maternity team today.”
avoid.why: Withholding time-critical treatment on assumption harms her recovery.

avoid.dont: “Come in when you can and we’ll have a look.”
avoid.instead: “Come in this morning — and if your arm or speech changes, call 999.”
avoid.why: Vague timing loses the 72-hour window and the stroke safety-net.

Contact us the same day for blisters around the ear, a painful or red eye, or change in vision, a severe headache, or feeling unwell with swelling or visual disturbance.
SCA_MODELS.why: Specific stroke, Ramsay Hunt, eye and pre-eclampsia safety-net

SCA_MODELS.text: Okay. I can get a lift in.
Just so I know I’ve explained it clearly — what’s the plan for this morning, and what would make you ring 999?
Come in now, protect my eye, and 999 if my arm or speech goes. And it’s probably not a stroke.
Exactly. You were right to ring. I’ll see you shortly.
SCA_MODELS.why: Closes with a clear next step

SCA_STEM.name: Priya Naidu
SCA_STEM.recent: Recent viral cold. Rang this morning: woke with the left side of her face drooping.
SCA_STEM.reason: Telephone call: “Half my face has dropped — is it a stroke?”

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE NG127 (suspected neurological conditions) · NICE NG128 (stroke and TIA) · NICE NG133 (hypertension in pregnancy)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Whole-hemiface weakness including the forehead, with no other neurology, points to Bell’s palsy — but sudden facial weakness still needs same-day examination. Treat early with prednisolone, protect the eye, and in pregnancy check for pre-eclampsia.

points.t: The upper face has bilateral cortical supply, so a stroke usually spares the forehead, while a lower motor neurone palsy weakens the whole side. It is a clue, not a complete test: a brainstem lesion can produce a whole-face palsy, so any other neurological sign goes to the stroke pathway (NICE NG128) whatever the forehead shows.

Acute unilateral lower motor neurone facial weakness developing over hours, often with ache behind the ear, altered taste or hyperacusis, after a viral illness. It is a diagnosis of exclusion: a typical story and an examination that is normal apart from the face.

Start oral prednisolone as early as possible, ideally within 72 hours of onset; regimen per local formulary and BNF. In pregnancy, discuss with the obstetric team but do not let the discussion delay treatment. Antivirals are not routine and never used alone.

Incomplete eye closure risks exposure keratopathy. Lubricating drops by day, ointment at night, gentle taping or a moisture chamber, and sunglasses. A painful or red eye or change in vision needs same-day ophthalmology.

Bell’s palsy is more common in late pregnancy, and published case series link it with gestational hypertension and pre-eclampsia. Check blood pressure and urine for protein at the same-day review and manage per NICE NG133.

Ramsay Hunt syndrome (ear or palate vesicles, severe ear pain, hearing loss, vertigo) needs antiviral plus steroid and urgent ENT input. Also consider Lyme disease, parotid masses and bilateral palsy. Review if not improving by about 3 weeks and consider facial-palsy referral at about 3 months if recovery is incomplete (local pathway); NICE NG127: consider specialist assessment for synkinesis from about 5 months.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; let her describe the onset and her fear before narrowing.
Pregnancy, what she saw happen to her nan, practical ability to attend today.
Picked up “I’m pregnant” and “my nan had one” and explored both.
Idea (stroke), concerns (the baby, treatment safety, permanent disfigurement), expectation (to know what it is and what to do).
Remote forehead and FAST checks; same-day face-to-face cranial and neurological examination, ear and mouth check, blood pressure and urine protein.
Bell’s palsy versus stroke, Ramsay Hunt, Lyme, parotid lesion; pregnancy-related hypertension.
Screened for limb, speech and visual deficits; knows a brainstem lesion can mimic a whole-face palsy; 999 route for any focal sign.
Probable Bell’s palsy, explained with the forehead reasoning, pending same-day examination.
Prednisolone within 72 hours with obstetric input, eye protection, no routine antiviral, honest prognosis.
Pregnancy: BP and urine check for pre-eclampsia, maternity-team liaison on steroids.
999 for stroke features; same-day contact for vesicles, eye pain or visual change; review if not improving.

social.t: Facial asymmetry, drooling and difficulty eating can be distressing and socially isolating. Acknowledge it and give a realistic recovery timeline.
A relative’s stroke shapes how she reads her own symptoms. Addressing that story directly reduces panic and improves engagement with the plan.

legal.t: If she cannot close the eye or protect it, or her vision is affected by drops or ointment, advise her not to drive until she can do so safely and meets the DVLA eyesight standard.
If she works and needs time off, a fit note can be issued; pregnancy-related protections at work continue alongside.

professional.t: Telephone triage can guide urgency but cannot replace examination for sudden neurological symptoms. Document the questions asked, the answers, and the plan for same-day review.
Weigh benefit and risk, check the BNF, involve the maternity team, and record the shared decision (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024).

community.t: Inform her midwife or maternity unit so blood pressure and fetal wellbeing are followed up at routine and additional antenatal visits.
Facial Palsy UK offers information on eye care, exercises and recovery, and support for people with persistent weakness.

redFlags: Limb weakness, speech or visual disturbance, ataxia or sensory loss — stroke pathway, 999
Vesicles in or around the ear or palate, severe ear pain, hearing loss or vertigo — Ramsay Hunt
Headache, visual disturbance, swelling or raised BP in pregnancy — possible pre-eclampsia
psychosocial: Pregnancy at 28 weeks and her fear for the baby
Her nan’s stroke and how it shapes her fear
Practical ability to attend today; eating, drinking and eye care at home
ice: Idea: “I’m having a stroke, like my nan”
Concern: harm to the baby from the illness or its treatment; permanent disfigurement
Expectation: to know whether it’s a stroke and what to do now

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Probable Bell’s palsy: the whole left face including the forehead is weak, with no limb, speech or visual deficit — but it still needs same-day examination: “This looks much more like a facial-nerve problem than a stroke. I want to examine you today to be sure.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “The facial nerve is like a cable from the brain to the face. In Bell’s palsy the cable itself becomes swollen and stops carrying signals to that whole side of the face — forehead included. In a stroke, the forehead usually keeps working because it gets a back-up signal from the other side of the brain.”

management.reflectIce: “You were frightened this was a stroke like your nan’s, and worried for the baby. The signs point to Bell’s palsy, which doesn’t harm the baby — and we’ll check you properly today.”
management.psychosocial: Make same-day attendance easy, give practical eye-care steps she can do now, and link in the maternity team so she isn’t carrying the pregnancy worry alone.
sharedPlan: Same-day face-to-face examination; BP and urine protein
Prednisolone within 72 hours per formulary and BNF, agreed with the maternity team
Eye protection: drops, night ointment, taping, sunglasses
safetyNet: 999 for limb weakness, speech change or drowsiness
Same-day contact for ear vesicles, eye pain or visual change, severe headache; review if no improvement

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This telephone station is about safe triage under emotional pressure: recognise the likely Bell’s palsy, still get her examined today, and deal with two fears — stroke and the baby.

items.fail: Confirming Bell’s palsy on the phone and posting a prescription without examination.
items.why: Sudden facial weakness needs examination to exclude stroke and Ramsay Hunt. The forehead clue is not a complete test — brainstem lesions can mimic it.
items.fix: “It looks much more like Bell’s, but I want to examine you this morning.”

items.why: Exposure keratopathy is a preventable complication and a commonly missed checkpoint.
items.fix: Drops by day, ointment and taping at night, sunglasses — and same-day review for eye pain or visual change.

items.fail: Refusing or delaying steroids because she is pregnant.
items.why: Benefit is time-dependent. Pregnancy calls for obstetric input, not automatic refusal.
items.fix: Offer prednisolone within 72 hours and agree it with the maternity team the same day.

items.fail: Treating the face in isolation and not checking blood pressure.
items.why: Bell’s palsy in late pregnancy has been linked with pre-eclampsia; missing it is a safety failure.
items.fix: BP and urine protein at the same-day review, and pre-eclampsia symptoms in the safety-net.

items.fail: Answering only the stroke question and never asking about the baby.
items.why: “Does not explore the patient’s concerns.” The unspoken pregnancy fear drives her distress.
items.fix: “Is there anything on your mind about the baby?”

items.why: “Language not easily understood by the patient”, especially on the phone.
items.fix: “In a stroke the forehead usually keeps working because it gets signals from both sides of the brain.”

items.fail: Safety-net limited to “call back if worse”.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting is standard failing feedback when stroke is on the differential.
items.fix: Name 999 symptoms (limb, speech, drowsiness) and same-day symptoms (ear vesicles, eye pain, visual change, severe headache).
